settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: MonitoringFilter.doMonitoring does check access with isRequestAllowed(httpRequest) and sends SC_FORBIDDEN otherwise, and CollectorServlet.doGet/doPost do call isAddressNotAllowed, so an access-control mechanism exists when the pattern parameter is set.
CollectorServlet.doPost does validate that appUrls starts with http:// or https://, which blocks non-HTTP schemes (e.g. file:, jar:).

RemoteCollector.dispatchSerializables only reacts to known types (Counter, JavaInformations, String, CounterRequestContext), which is some post-deserialization narrowing but does not prevent gadget execution during readObject/fromXML.
candidates.description:
CollectorServlet.doPost reads 'appName' and 'appUrls' straight from the request and, after only a prefix check that appUrls starts with 'http://' or 'https://', calls collectorController.addCollectorApplication(appName, appUrls). The only access control is isAddressNotAllowed(req), which returns false whenever 'allowedAddrPattern' is null (i.e. whenever no allowed-addr-pattern parameter is configured, which is the default). CollectorController.addCollectorApplication then parses the URLs and forwards them to collectorServer.addCollectorApplication; the collector server stores them and RemoteCollector later issues HTTP GETs to those URLs, taking the response body and passing it to TransportFormat.readSerializableFrom. In the SERIALIZED format that method wraps the response in a java.io.ObjectInputStream and calls readObject(); in the XML format it builds an XStream instance and calls fromXML. As a result, anyone able to reach the collector servlet (no authentication is visible in the read code) can register a URL pointing at a server they control and have the collector server deserialize attacker-supplied data, which is the classic gadget-chain / external-entity exposure surface. Under the read code the data is trusted only so far as the operator ensures every polled URL is trusted; the default configuration does not enforce that.

Note: transport format choice, XStream version (older, from pom.xml), and whether the collector servlet is deployed behind additional authentication are outside the read spans, so this is reported as a candidate, not a confirmed vulnerability.
missing_evidence: Whether the collector server is typically fronted by a servlet-container authentication realm or other access control (web.xml / web-fragment.xml were not read).
The XStream version actually on the collector server classpath at runtime (pom.xml references an old XStream, but that file was not among the inspected spans).
Whether a Java serialization filter (ObjectInputFilter / jdk.serialFilter) is configured anywhere.
Whether adding applications requires any CSRF token or session in practice.
The exact behavior of CollectorServer.addCollectorApplication/RemoteCollector.collectForUrl (not within the read spans).
preconditions: Collector server webapp (CollectorServlet) is deployed and reachable by the attacker.
Parameter ALLOWED_ADDR_PATTERN is not configured (default), so isAddressNotAllowed() returns false.
The collector's application-add form is reachable without an additional authentication layer (not visible in the read source).
The attacker can make the collector poll a URL they control that returns a crafted Java-serialized (or XML) payload.
candidates.title: CollectorServlet POST adds a caller-controlled application URL (http/https only) that is later fetched and deserialized without authentication

counter_evidence: The XML/JSON paths only execute if the corresponding library (XStream, XPP3) is present; checkDependencies() throws a RuntimeException otherwise.
The JSON format's read path throws UnsupportedOperationException, so JSON is not a read-side deserialization surface.
In the read code all inputs originate from configured collector URLs, i.e. inside the trusted monitoring network in the normal deployment model.
candidates.description: TransportFormat.readSerializableFrom selects a deserializer based on the enum value: for SERIALIZED it creates 'new ObjectInputStream(bufferedInput)' and calls readObject(); for XML it delegates to XmlIO.readFromXml, which creates an XStream instance via createXStream(false) and calls xstream.fromXML(reader). createXStream only registers a permissive MapConverter (canConvert always returns true) and aliases, and no allow-list, no ObjectInputFilter, and no XStream security framework setup is visible in the read code. Any data reaching readSerializableFrom from an untrusted or attacker-influencable source (for example the response of a collector-polled URL) would be deserialized with the full class graph exposed by the classpath. This is reported separately from the request-handling candidate above because the dangerous deserialization primitive is the root cause regardless of which caller supplies the stream.
missing_evidence: No evidence in the read spans that a JDK serialization filter or XStream security configuration is set elsewhere.
Actual XStream version/patches at runtime not confirmed in the read spans.
The callers of readSerializableFrom that pass non-collector-controlled streams were not all inspected.
preconditions: An input stream reaching TransportFormat.readSerializableFrom contains attacker-controlled bytes.
The chosen transport format is SERIALIZED or XML.
A gadget or malicious XML payload matching classes on the classpath is available to the attacker.
candidates.title: TransportFormat deserializes collector data with raw ObjectInputStream / XStream.fromXML (no type or class allow-listing visible)
